John F. Kennedy's inauguration. On January 20, 1961, John F. Kennedy became the youngest elected president and the first Catholic to take office. At 43 years old, he delivered an inaugural address that galvanized a generation with its vision of American idealism and sacrifice. Kennedy urged Americans with a call that would echo through decades: ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country. He called for global cooperation against tyranny and outlined an ambitious new initiative called the Peace Corps, a civilian volunteer program that would embody American idealism. He addressed the Soviet Union directly during the height of Cold War tensions. Let us never negotiate out of fear, he declared, but let us never fear to negotiate, promising American strength while seeking dialogue. His address inspired massive civic participation and optimism particularly among young people. The poet Robert Frost was invited to participate in the ceremony, reading "The Gift Outright," adding cultural gravitas to the moment. Kennedy's inaugural address emphasized American idealism and democratic duty while directly confronting the nuclear-age realities of superpower competition and the possibility of mutual annihilation.
